routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is reasonable through a cumulative historical inference from Jesus' death, the reported empty tomb and appearances, witness transformations, early proclamation, and comparison with rival explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its principal historical claims are adequately supported, bodily resurrection explains their conjunction better than the live alternatives, and the evidential standard permits supernatural causation to be inferred without first assuming it.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative historical and explanatory case to the conclusion that belief in Jesus' bodily resurrection is epistemically reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish the material historical data concerning death, burial or the empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and early resurrection proclamation.
Show that bodily resurrection has greater explanatory scope and power than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, error, or combinations of natural alternatives.
Show that the event's religious context and the failure of competing explanations warrant identifying the resurrection as divine action.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the historical sources through their asserted earliness, multiplicity, local detail, cultural fit, archaeology, and relevant scholarly agreement.
Defend ordinary cumulative historical reasoning against standards alleged to exclude extraordinary conclusions categorically or generate an evidential regress.

routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is unreasonable because transmitted reports, disputed historical premises, and background compatibility do not provide sufficient warrant for either the event or its supernatural cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available sources do not adequately establish the material premises, ordinary explanations or unresolved uncertainty remain live, or the evidence fails to meet the burden appropriate to an extraordinary supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the insufficiency and underdetermination of the available evidence to withholding belief in bodily resurrection as the reasonable position.

centralBridges.description: Show that late, dependent, disputed, or second- and third-hand reports cannot securely establish the proposed resurrection facts.
Show that sincerity, movement growth, accurate background details, and reported experiences remain compatible with legend, error, transmission, or unknown causes.
Require evidence not only that an unusual event occurred but also that resurrection was possible and that supernatural or divine causation produced it.
Apply an evidential burden proportionate to the extraordinariness and low background plausibility of bodily resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish reports, sincere beliefs, and incidental historical accuracy from independent support for the resurrection proposition itself.
Defend suspension of judgment without requiring a complete rival reconstruction or a claim that resurrection is impossible.

sections.title: Historical facts and source reliability
sections.rationale: The cumulative inference depends on whether death, burial, the empty tomb, appearances, conversions, and early proclamation are established by sufficiently early, independent, consistent, and reliable sources.

sections.title: Testimony, sincerity, and corroboration
sections.rationale: The parties dispute what reported experiences, costly commitment, local knowledge, archaeology, and accurate background details can establish about the central resurrection claims.

sections.title: Resurrection and rival explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether resurrection explains the proposed historical data better than legend, deception, hallucination, error, transmission, combined alternatives, or unresolved uncertainty.

sections.title: Event evidence and supernatural causation
sections.rationale: Evidence for an unusual return to life and evidence that God caused a bodily resurrection are distinct inferential questions whose connection is necessary to the motion.

sections.title: Extraordinary claims and evidential burden
sections.rationale: The appropriate relationship among prior plausibility, extraordinary claims, proportional evidence, and historical inference determines what support reasonable belief requires.

sections.title: Reasonable belief and suspension of judgment
sections.rationale: The ultimate burden requires deciding whether the cumulative case warrants belief or whether remaining evidential uncertainty makes suspension of judgment the justified motion-level conclusion.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Belief in Jesus' resurrection can be reasonable when likely historical facts are established and competing explanations of those facts are compared cumulatively.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike begins his uninterrupted opening statement at event 155 and explicitly presents this two-part case in the first person.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines the two-stage cumulative method used to connect historical premises and explanatory comparison to reasonable belief.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly establishes the governing method and motion-level destination.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-part method and its probabilistic historical threshold are clearly recoverable and consistently scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It claims that belief can be reasonable under stated conditions, rather than claiming the method already proves resurrection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional structure is coherent, though the standards for likely facts and best explanation remain to be supplied later.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies a defensible framework but, as an introductory methodological statement, does not yet substantiate its premises.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly connects the entire cumulative route to the motion-level reasonableness conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents a positive framework without materially characterizing a live opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly announces a two-part case based on likely first-century facts and a subsequent explanatory comparison.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Jesus' death by Roman crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is a securely supported historical foundation for assessing the resurrection claim.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has yielded the floor to Mike, who labels this the first fact and supports it by invoking historical sources and scholarly testimony.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the death premise required before a bodily resurrection inference can be considered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly establishes a necessary historical datum with named scholarly support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claimed event, agent, and official context are clear, though the precise independence standard is compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confidence broadly fits the cited consensus claim, but source independence and the eleven-source count are not defended here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cited historical agreement and multiple-source claim coherently support crucifixion as a foundational datum.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named scholarly testimony and an asserted source count provide support, with a bounded independence-verification gap.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Death by crucifixion is an indispensable component of the central historical-data bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: No meaningful rival interpretation is developed in this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Roman crucifixion under Pilate, invokes Bart Ehrman, and asserts eleven independent supporting sources.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Jesus was probably buried in a private tomb later found empty, supported by considerations including multiple attestation, women witnesses, Joseph of Arimathea, and archaeology.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike explicitly introduces burial and the empty tomb as his third and fourth facts, then supplies six consecutive supporting considerations and a conclusion.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies burial and empty-tomb premises central to the proposed bodily-resurrection inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops several concrete considerations for two important historical premises.

precisionFindings.rationale: The probability claim and its several supporting considerations are identifiable and appropriately qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic framing is suitable, but attestation independence and the women-witness inference receive compressed treatment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The considerations are cumulatively relevant, although none alone entails burial in a private tomb or discovery empty.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple attestation, Joseph, women witnesses, and archaeology are specific support, but key reliability warrants remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Burial and an empty tomb are major components of the central historical-data bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances positive historical considerations without a developed competing account to test charitably.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span develops women witnesses, Joseph of Arimathea, multiple attestation, and archaeological considerations for burial and emptiness.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Individual and group experiences understood as appearances of the risen Jesus form historical data that ordinary hallucination does not adequately explain.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike identifies this as his fifth historical fact and develops it continuously through named accounts, scholarly consensus claims, and the hallucination inference.

response.rationale: This constructive move presents appearance experiences as data and uses their individual and group character against a simple hallucination account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a major datum and begins explicit rival comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move distinguishes experiences interpreted as appearances from the further resurrection conclusion and identifies its rival target.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Confidence that experiences occurred has named support, while the inadequacy of hallucination is less fully demonstrated.

charity.alternative: The witnesses had individual or socially reinforced experiences without an external risen body.
charity.decisiveQualification: Group reports require source and phenomenological scrutiny before ordinary hallucination is excluded.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Reported experiences are relevant data, but the bridge from group reports to failure of hallucination remains partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named scholarly agreement supports post-death experiences, with material gaps about report independence and group phenomenology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports resurrection's comparative explanatory power against a named natural rival.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes hallucination as a live rival but treats the group-report consideration too quickly as decisive.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes individual and group experiences and quotes Lüdemann treating post-death appearance experiences as historically certain.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: The disciples' transformed lives and willingness to endure persecution support the inference that they sincerely believed they had encountered the risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike continues his opening, introduces transformation as the next fact, and resumes the same argument after a brief technical interruption about his slides.

response.rationale: This constructive move supports sincere belief through transformation, persecution, and named early adherents.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it materially supports sincerity while appropriately stopping short of making sincerity prove truth.

precisionFindings.rationale: The sincerity inference is recoverable, but the span shifts between broad disciples and especially supported named individuals.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Costly commitment supports sincerity, though the broad willingness-to-die formulation exceeds the specifically named support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Transformation and accepted persecution coherently support sincerity, though they do not independently establish what caused the belief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple-source and named-person support is asserted, but the evidence for the broader disciple group is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Sincerity and transformation materially contribute to the central historical-data bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move argues for sincerity and does not meaningfully characterize an opposing explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites transformed lives, persecution, and especially Peter, James, and Paul as support for sincere resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Jesus' religious, miraculous, and prophetic context indicates that, if he rose, the event is best understood as an act of God.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike introduces religious significance as his tenth fact and expressly draws the inference that the context identifies God as the resurrection's cause.

response.rationale: This constructive move attempts the necessary bridge from an unusual return to life to specifically divine action.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it expressly addresses causal identification rather than leaving divine agency assumed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional claim is clear, but religious context, miracle, and prophecy are grouped without a stable evidential distinction.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The if-he-rose qualification is explicit, but contextual fit alone does not strongly identify God as the cause.

charity.alternative: Jesus returned to life through an unknown cause not identifiable as divine action.
charity.decisiveQualification: Religious context can favor an interpretation without independently identifying the causal mechanism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Religious context is evidentially relevant, but the causal bridge from contextual significance to divine agency remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Prophetic and miraculous context is asserted, while independent support and comparison with unknown causation are underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the indispensable central bridge identifying divine causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the nond divine-cause possibility but understates the remaining causal underdetermination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that the religious and prophetic context surrounding Jesus indicates God caused the event if resurrection occurred.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Resurrection explains the cumulative historical data better than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, or combinations of those natural rival explanations.
moves.attributionBasis: Mike explicitly shifts from listing facts to asking for their best explanation and consecutively evaluates the resurrection and several named alternatives.

response.rationale: This constructive move performs the central explanatory comparison between resurrection and several named natural alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it squarely addresses the route's decisive comparative-explanation requirement.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative conclusion and named rivals are recoverable, though the criteria for 'better' remain partly implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is stronger than the excerpt's compressed dismissal of separate and combined natural alternatives warrants.

charity.alternative: A combination of error, legend, altered transmission, and sincere experiences explains different portions of the data.
charity.decisiveQualification: A combined rival may sacrifice simplicity while avoiding commitment to an otherwise unsupported resurrection mechanism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Inference to the best explanation is valid in form, but comparative criteria and exhaustive rival treatment remain materially incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names serious alternatives yet largely asserts their inadequacy without representative evidence or sustained comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is direct, high-position contact with the central explanation-comparison bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Named rivals are considered, but their strongest combined forms and evidential tradeoffs are treated too briefly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span announces best-explanation analysis and addresses conspiracy, hallucination, legend, and combinations as alternatives.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Sincere testimony can support that an extraordinary experience was reported without sufficiently establishing that its supernatural interpretation is true.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening turn is explicitly handed to Matt immediately before the core, and the first-person family example remains within that turn.

components.text: Whether sincere, costly belief establishes the truth of the witnesses' supernatural interpretation.
Whether reports of appearance experiences establish that a bodily resurrection actually occurred.

response.rationale: The reply distinguishes evidence that people reported or believed an experience from evidence that the supernatural interpretation is true, stating the defeating consequence for both sincerity and appearance reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies the evidential conflation and states why the cited testimony cannot by itself establish resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: Claims, testimony, experience, and supernatural truth are consistently distinguished throughout the move.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited necessity claim—that testimony alone does not prove its supernatural interpretation—fits the stated distinction.

charity.alternative: Sincere testimony is cumulative evidence rather than a standalone deductive proof of resurrection.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its evidential value remains limited without independent support connecting the experience to an external risen body.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between a report, sincere belief, and the truth of its interpretation is explicit and inferentially sound.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual warrant is strong, though the reply does not quantify how much cumulative evidential weight testimony retains.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary bridge distinguishing claims and sincerity from proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly preserves testimonial relevance while denying that it independently establishes the supernatural conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says the reports are claims about resurrection and distinguishes those claims from evidence establishing resurrection.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Resurrection cannot serve as the best explanation unless the possibility of supernatural interaction is supported rather than exempted from ordinary evidential standards.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker remains Matt throughout the con opening and frames the passage in his established skeptical vocabulary of evidence, possibility, and special pleading.

components.text: Whether resurrection is an eligible best-explanation candidate without support that supernatural interaction is possible.
Whether religious context supplies evidence that a supernatural cause can interact with reality.

response.rationale: The reply directly imposes an eligibility condition on the proposed supernatural explanation and denies that contextual labeling substitutes for evidence of possible interaction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the decisive candidate-eligibility issue, though it does not specify what evidence would satisfy the demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The demand is clear, but 'supernatural is real' and 'can interact' compress distinct modal and causal questions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some causal warrant is necessary, but demanding prior proof of the supernatural may set the threshold too categorically.

charity.alternative: A well-supported event could itself contribute evidence for a previously uncertain supernatural causal category.
charity.decisiveQualification: The event evidence must still discriminate supernatural causation from unknown natural causation rather than merely assume the label.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The need for causal warrant is coherent, while the prior-demonstration requirement risks an unsupported sequencing condition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The epistemic demand is reasoned but not supported by a developed account of possibility evidence or candidate thresholds.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central requirement for warranted causal identification.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the causal-warrant problem but underplays the possibility of event evidence and causal evidence developing jointly.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt requires evidence that the supernatural is real and interacts with reality before treating it as an explanation.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Known sources of false reports, including deception, legend, error, and exaggeration, remain better-grounded candidates than an unsupported resurrection mechanism.
moves.attributionBasis: This is still Matt's uninterrupted opening, with first-person methodological language and an explicit appeal to Hume consistent with the surrounding con argument.

components.text: Whether resurrection outranks known mechanisms producing false or exaggerated reports.
Whether labeling God special establishes a viable causal mechanism rather than special pleading.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges resurrection's comparative eligibility by contrasting it with known report-generating mechanisms and demanding demonstration of viability.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the best-explanation comparison, though the excerpt develops the natural candidates less fully than the objection to resurrection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is recoverable, but 'magic' rhetorically merges divine agency with an unspecified mechanism.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Known error mechanisms deserve prior weight, but the move does not compare their fit to each proposed datum in detail.

charity.alternative: Resurrection is proposed as a specific personal cause inferred from the conjunction of data, not as generic magic.
charity.decisiveQualification: Specific labeling does not remove the need to show viability and comparative explanatory advantage.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Known mechanisms rationally receive evidential consideration, though prior familiarity alone cannot decide comparative fit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies familiar mechanisms but offers little case-specific evidence that any one or combination explains the data.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central claim that resurrection is the superior explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The core viability challenge survives, but calling the proposal magic materially weakens the strongest causal formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span contrasts a supernatural mechanism with known sources of false reports and demands evidence that resurrection is viable.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Noncontemporary and source-dependent accounts with unresolved inconsistencies do not securely convert the proposed minimal-facts list into established historical facts.
moves.attributionBasis: The con opening continues without interruption, and Matt explicitly names Michael, Gary Habermas, the minimal-facts approach, and his own predebate stipulations.

components.text: Whether late, dependent, and inconsistent accounts securely establish burial and empty-tomb facts.
Whether transmitted appearance accounts are sufficiently early and independent to establish the proposed data.
Whether the cited source base independently verifies the proposed historical foundation.

response.rationale: The reply challenges the source properties required to turn the proposed minimal facts into established data, reaching several historical premises rather than merely objecting generally.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the source-sufficiency demand across the historical case, with some specific inconsistencies and dependence concerns.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source critique is clear, though its broad conclusion sometimes ranges across premises with different evidential support.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that the facts are not securely established, a force proportionate to the stated dependence and inconsistency concerns.

charity.alternative: Late sources may preserve earlier traditions and can retain historical value despite literary dependence.
charity.decisiveQualification: Their value still depends on tracing early material and avoiding double-counting dependent attestations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Source lateness, dependence, and unresolved inconsistency coherently reduce confidence in asserted historical facts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The critique identifies concrete source features, though the excerpt does not document every premise or dependency claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central bridge testing whether the historical sources securely establish the data.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply does not simply discard late sources; its decisive concern is whether their evidential independence has been shown.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked span discusses the minimal-facts presentation while challenging noncontemporary accounts, dependence, and unresolved inconsistencies.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Rejecting selected natural alternatives does not establish resurrection when information is incomplete and unknown possibilities remain, so insufficient evidence warrants uncertainty.
moves.attributionBasis: This passage forms the closing sequence of Matt's opening, ending immediately before the moderator announces the transition to dialogue and summarizes his conclusion.

components.text: Whether eliminating selected rivals establishes resurrection as the best explanation under incomplete information.
Whether cumulative comparison warrants belief when relevant information and possible explanations remain unknown.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the inference from rejected options to resurrection as unreliable under incomplete information and states uncertainty and nonacceptance as the consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the failure in eliminative reasoning and gives a clear motion-level defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully distinguishes denying occurrence from denying that current evidence makes belief reasonable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The underdetermination point is strong, although 'absolutely not reasonable' is firmer than the illustrative argument alone establishes.

charity.alternative: Inference to the best explanation need not exhaust every logically possible alternative.
charity.decisiveQualification: It must still compare the strongest live alternatives and justify the proposed candidate despite acknowledged informational gaps.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between eliminating selected options and establishing a conclusion is explicit and logically well supported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The information-gap illustration supports the inference, though its fit to each historical datum is not fully developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly connects evidential underdetermination to the motion-level conclusion that belief should be withheld.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves abductive reasoning in principle while showing why incomplete elimination cannot alone complete it here.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses an incomplete-information illustration and expressly concludes that insufficient evidence does not warrant resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Detailed knowledge of Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs cumulatively corroborates the historical reliability of the Gospel reporting.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn advances the resurrection defender's case, directly addresses Matt, and is followed by Matt's explicit skeptical rebuttal.

components.text: Whether incidental local accuracy gives the Gospel reports evidential value beyond bare unsupported claims.
Whether detailed Palestinian knowledge corroborates source reliability despite proposed lateness.

response.rationale: The reply supplies local institutional, geographic, and customary details as corroboration against treating the narratives as mere unsupported assertions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts source reliability and the claims-versus-support distinction, but does not bridge incidental accuracy to the central miracle report.

precisionFindings.rationale: The local-detail claim is clear, but the scope shifts from corroborating background knowledge to broader narrative reliability.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Accurate local details support contextual knowledge but do not by themselves strongly validate resurrection reporting.

charity.alternative: A source can preserve accurate local detail while remaining mistaken, legendary, or dependent concerning its central claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: Incidental corroboration increases some source confidence without transferring automatically to extraordinary content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Local detail is relevant corroboration, but the move substantially compresses the bridge to general Gospel reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several concrete examples are offered, yet their independence, dating, and relevance to resurrection are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary corroboration bridge, near the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply gives little weight to the decisive distinction between background accuracy and central-event reliability.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites knowledge of Zacchaeus, Palestinian institutions, geography, and customs as cumulative confirmatory details.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: A case combining reasonably established nonmiraculous historical facts with resurrection as their best explanation need not prove its conclusion before its supporting evidence is considered.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker identifies his own two-part case and directly characterizes Matt's epistemic objection as circular, clearly marking Mike's turn.

components.text: Whether supernatural possibility must be independently proved before historical evidence and explanatory fit can be considered.
Whether objections should address the specific nonmiraculous historical premises rather than dismiss the whole case generally.
Whether the case is a two-stage abductive argument rather than bare elimination of rivals.

response.rationale: The reply justifies evaluating ordinary historical premises first and resurrection's explanatory performance second, preserving the causal issue without requiring the conclusion before evidence is considered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly replaces a prior-proof demand with a two-stage evidential test and explains why that reframe preserves the legitimate issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two parts, their order, and the distinction between premise criticism and explanatory criticism are clearly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that evidence may be assessed before its conclusion is proved is appropriately categorical.

charity.alternative: The skeptical demand concerns adequate warrant for supernatural candidacy, not proof of the final conclusion in advance.
charity.decisiveQualification: That demand can be preserved at the explanatory stage without blocking assessment of ordinary historical premises.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The separation of historical premises from later explanatory comparison is explicit and resolves much of the sequencing objection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological defense is well reasoned, with the substantive adequacy of each stage necessarily left to other moves.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It is very strong contact within the subsidiary evidential-standard bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly reconstructs two kinds of objection, though its circularity suggestion slightly overstates the opponent's position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly separates reasonably believable nonmiraculous facts from the later claim that resurrection best explains them.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Concluding that resurrection has not met its burden is compatible with leaving its occurrence possible and does not assume that supernatural events cannot occur.
moves.attributionBasis: The direct correction of Mike's circularity charge and the first-person statement of the skeptical conclusion identify Matt's responsive turn.

components.text: Whether withholding belief for an unmet burden circularly assumes that resurrection or the supernatural cannot occur.

response.rationale: The reply defines circularity, denies that its conclusion entails impossibility, and states that an unmet burden supports nonacceptance rather than denial.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly answers the circularity charge at its decisive premise and gives the exact skeptical conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: Occurrence, possibility, burden satisfaction, and nonacceptance are sharply and consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conceptual claim about nonacceptance follows from the stated burden without asserting that resurrection is impossible.

charity.alternative: The pro objection may target an evidential standard that functionally excludes supernatural explanations rather than formal circularity.
charity.decisiveQualification: That broader objection requires showing exclusion; it does not make simple burden-based nonacceptance circular.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between not accepting a claim and asserting its negation is explicit, consistent, and decisive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response is primarily conceptual and supplies the required definitions and consequence with only a minor application gap.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level bridge from unmet warrant to withholding resurrection belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the stated circularity allegation accurately while leaving room for a separate standards critique.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines circular reasoning and explicitly says the conclusion is unmet burden, not impossibility or nonoccurrence.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The reported crucifixion lacks contemporary verification, while the absence of independent reports for associated conspicuous events weakens confidence in the narrative source.
moves.attributionBasis: The skeptical first-person assessment follows Mike's request for agreement and invokes Matt's recurring source-verification and independent-attestation standards.

components.text: Whether contemporary or independent evidence verifies Jesus' reported crucifixion and associated narrative claims.
Whether incidental narrative detail overcomes the absence of expected independent reports for conspicuous events.

response.rationale: The reply directly contests verification of the crucifixion account and appeals to missing contemporary and expected independent reporting.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the claimed historical foundation, although it does not engage the specifically cited later sources or consensus evidence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contemporary-account point is clear, but 'storybook whose veracity cannot be verified' ranges beyond the evidence discussed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Absence of contemporary verification lowers confidence but does not alone warrant the broad unverifiability characterization.

charity.alternative: Ancient events can be historically well supported by later sources, especially when multiple and independently grounded.
charity.decisiveQualification: The pro side must still demonstrate actual independence and explain missing expected contemporary corroboration.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The absence-of-expected-evidence inference is coherent but needs an explicit expectation and preservation-rate warrant.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific absences are identified, while the probability of surviving Roman or contemporary documentation is not established.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central source-sufficiency bridge regarding a foundational historical datum.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves a legitimate verification demand but gives insufficient weight to ordinary historical reliance on later sources.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies contemporary accounts and points to the absence of expected Roman and independent reporting.

moves.speaker: Mike Winger
moves.proposition: Paul's language and relevant Jewish historical concepts indicate that the earliest resurrection claim concerned Jesus' bodily resurrection rather than a merely spectral experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn presents Pauline passages and a scholarly word study for the pro position before Matt objects that Mike is defending an unasserted target.

components.text: Whether the underlying event reports are independently and contemporaneously verified.
Whether the earliest claim meant bodily resurrection rather than a merely spectral experience.

response.rationale: The move clarifies what Paul and relevant Jewish concepts meant by resurrection, but it does not answer the immediately decisive verification problem or establish that the bodily event occurred.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a material answer to a secondary interpretive issue while leaving the primary historical-verification demand uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Bodily resurrection is consistently contrasted with a spectral experience, making the interpretive proposition clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: 'No way around it' is stronger than the compressed word-study and historical-concept support presented in the span.

charity.alternative: Pauline resurrection language might permit a transformed spiritual body without implying an ordinary resuscitated corpse.
charity.decisiveQualification: The relevant Jewish and Pauline usage still concerns embodied resurrection, though the nature of that body requires qualification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Linguistic and historical concepts coherently bear on meaning, while meaning does not establish occurrence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Pauline language and a scholarly word study provide support, but competing interpretations are not examined in depth.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the subsidiary distinction between the content of claims and support for their truth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move addresses a spectral reading but states the bodily conclusion more categorically than the interpretive nuance permits.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span invokes Pauline wording, a word study, and Jewish concepts to argue that the earliest claim concerned bodily resurrection.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Paul's third-party reports of appearances do not establish that the named witnesses personally attested as claimed or that a resurrection actually occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker resumes the answer interrupted by the Paul discussion and explicitly contrasts what Saul believed with what is true or evidentially supported.

components.text: Whether establishing Paul's bodily meaning establishes that the reported resurrection actually happened.
Whether Paul's third-party list establishes personal witness attestation and the truth of the appearances.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the shift from what Paul believed or meant to what evidence establishes as true, and states that third-party reporting does not close that gap.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly diagnoses the belief-to-truth inference and applies the consequence to Paul's reported witnesses.

precisionFindings.rationale: Paul's belief, third-party reporting, witness attestation, and event truth are clearly differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that belief content alone does not establish truth is fully proportionate to the warrant.

charity.alternative: Paul's early report may provide some evidence of an established appearance tradition even without direct witness statements.
